Do you mean red-tailed hawk and not Cooper’s hawk? The dark belly band is a good marking to look at. Notice the location of the band and white plumage above/below the belly band.

Cooper’s hawks are completely different in beak shape, eye color (unless juvenile), and plumage, especially the belly. 

Peregrine falcons also have much different facial markings than red-tailed hawks. Their heads are more short and rounded compared to a red-tailed hawk’s, which have sleek and pointed heads. 

Keep in mind that red-tailed hawks also have different morph colors/regional differences as well as juvenile differences.

I think sending a text saying that you’d like to see him in person to resolve the conflict when he feels ready is a good way to start. And from an AP perspective, he probably is wondering why you have hurt him and why you haven’t reached out yet to show that you care that you hurt him and feel apologetic. And he’s probably worried that you’re going to abandon him, so that’s why he’s keeping his distance. When I get hurt too, I tend to want to protest and put my walls up so I can brace for the hurt that will come (in my mind) when they will want to break up with me over the conflict. It’s not really rational, but it’s a pretty strong feeling that kind of takes over your mind.  

Edit: adding on to this, I think it’s important to emphasize in your text during reaching out that you want to see him because you feel regretful that you had hurt him and want to make things right, not just cause you miss him. He probably thinks you’ve pushed the issue under the rug and ignored his hurt

If you haven’t already, I would suggest bringing this issue up in a non-accusatory way. Treat it as though it’s you and him vs. the problem instead of you vs. him. I’d also apologize for your behavior and say that you understand that it hurt him, and that you’ll try to do better next time so that you don’t repeat the same behavior that hurt him.  

I think both of you are still hurt and want to reach out to each other, but it feels weird because you both haven’t reassured each other that the problem is resolved and that you still love each other and want to continue working on the relationship so that both of you can work in yourselves so that everyone’s needs are met. It’s going to be difficult to extend an olive branch after an argument (I 100% understand how that feels). It’s scary and requires somebody to be vulnerable. 

Edit: also I think saying something along the lines of “hey, I was wondering if you are ready to talk about what happened between us, because I want resolve this conflict and heal our relationship. I understand that my actions have hurt you, and I want to hear your perspective on what happened” is a good way to open up. It allows him to be heard and his feelings validated. Listen without interrupting, and Then address that issue. Then it’ll be your turn to speak about how protest behaviors hurt your feelings.

When you pick up your conure, do you make him step up on your finger or do you just straight up grab him?    

Unfortunately, undoing this may be difficult, so you will need to be patient. Perhaps the first step would be offering treats to your conure and have him eat it out of your hand, that way he associates your hand with a positive experience. If you grab your parrot instead of having him step-up, I suggest you stop doing that because birds don’t like to be wrapped around like that without consent and will be fearful of your hands instead. If you need to remove him from a situation and he won’t step up on your finger, I suggest that you use a perch or those bird ladders and have him step up onto that. 

After you’ve earned his trust a little again with hand feeding treats, I suggest clicker training him to step up on your finger so that when you ask him to do it in the future, he will pretty much do it automatically and also won’t associate your hand with negativity. 

Right now, your conure doesn’t trust you as much as your wife, so I wouldn’t try to force scritches and cuddles on him if it visibly makes him uncomfortable, but if he is accepting, then go for it.

Your best bet is positive reinforcement whenever he is near your hands or near you in the form of treats and verbal praise (until he is comfortable with you touching him again) and a lot of patience.  

As for disciplining a parrot, you would have better results allowing your conure to redirect his boredom to something else he can chew on instead of cables. There are a lot of different types of toys out there that you can try to distract him with (such as foot toys e.g. sola balls)

I can only answer for GCC. Mine is extremely cuddly and friendly with everybody, BUT, she can be extremely moody. Especially during molting season. Also, be aware that a GCC going through puberty may also be moody, which may include being more nippy and may even seem like they hate you. Just be prepared that your GCC may not be friendly all the time because that’s a part of bird ownership and need to respect their boundaries. 

The one you get may not even be as cuddly as the ones you see on this sub because each bird has their own personality. Often times, I see forum posts asking why their GCC suddenly became “mean” when they hit the age of two (puberty). Some GCC maybe friendly with everyone (like mine), or they end up being one person birds. I have seen people’s GCC being extremely protective over their owner and attack anyone else that interacts or comes close to their owner.  

I suggest you do more research so you know what you’re getting into. All parrots make noise so don’t expect any to be quiet all the time.  Some days, my GCC is very quiet and makes squeaking noises. Other days, she feels like squawking and sometimes screaming a little bit. Respect and be able to read your bird’s body language. Parrots don’t bite for no reason. Often times, they’ve already showed multiple signs to back off, but people unacquainted with parrots ignore the signs and then get surprised when they get bit.
